title: Dundee cake
subtitle: Scottish fruit cake with a blanched almond topping
excerpt: Dundee cake is a Scottish fruit cake enriched with butter, eggs, and dried fruit, finished with concentric rings of blanched almonds. It has a dense, moist crumb with a light almond crust on top. The almond topping must be pressed on gently before baking so it adheres without sinking.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (Book of Household Management, 1861). F. Marian McNeill (The Scots Kitchen, 1929, public domain). Traditional Scottish baking documented in various 19th-century household manuals.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap tightly in baking paper and foil and freeze for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dundee cake improves with keeping. Bake 2 to 3 days ahead and store in an airtight tin.
recipe.temperatureNote: conventional oven; low and slow for an even bake

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 160 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 145 degrees Celsius. Bake on the middle shelf.
baking.decoratingTechnique: Concentric rings of blanched almonds pressed onto the surface before baking

glossaryTerms.definition: Beating softened butter and sugar together until the mixture is pale, light, and fluffy before adding eggs and flour. The process incorporates air into the fat, which helps the cake rise. The butter must be genuinely soft, not melted, for the method to work.

Fruit with most of its moisture removed, used in baking for concentrated sweetness and chew. In fruit cakes, sultanas, currants, and glacé cherries are the most common. Dried fruit can be soaked in liquid overnight to plump it and prevent it scorching during a long bake.

folded in at the end. The almond topping is the defining feature; press each almond flat against the raw batter in neat rings and do not brush with egg until you are satisfied with the pattern.

Heat the oven to 160 degrees Celsius (conventional) or 145 degrees Celsius (fan). Grease a 20 cm round cake tin and line the base and sides with baking paper. A double layer on the sides protects the edges from the long bake.

Beat the butter and soft brown sugar together in a large bowl until pale and creamy, about 4 to 5 minutes with a hand mixer. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition. If the mixture starts to curdle, add a tablespoon of the flour.
Sift the flour and baking powder together and fold into the butter mixture with a large silicone spatula. Fold in the ground almonds, orange zest, and whisky or orange juice until combined.
Add the sultanas, currants, and halved glacé cherries and fold through evenly. The batter will be thick. Spoon into the prepared tin and level the surface with the back of a spoon.

Arrange the blanched almonds in concentric rings on the surface, pressing each one very lightly so it sits flat without sinking. Brush gently with a little beaten egg or water to help the nuts brown during baking.

Bake on the middle shelf for 85 to 90 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean and the almonds on top are a deep golden brown. Check at 75 minutes; if the top is browning too quickly, lay a sheet of baking paper loosely over the top.

Leave to cool in the tin for 20 minutes, then turn out onto a cooling rack and peel away the lining paper. Cool completely before slicing. Store in an airtight tin for up to 2 weeks; the flavour improves over the first 3 days.

attrs.problem: Almonds sink into the batter during baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid pressing the almonds in deeply; they should sit on the surface with only the barest pressure to keep them upright.
attrs.fix: Use whole blanched almonds rather than flaked, and lay them flat rather than standing on their ends. The batter is thick enough to support them as long as they are not pushed in.

attrs.problem: Top browns before the centre is cooked
attrs.avoid: Avoid placing the tin on the upper shelf.
attrs.fix: Bake on the middle shelf and cover loosely with a sheet of baking paper after 60 minutes if the top is colouring fast. The internal temperature should reach 95 degrees Celsius at the centre.

attrs.problem: Dried fruit sinks to the bottom
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding fruit to a very liquid batter.
attrs.fix: The batter for Dundee cake is intentionally thick; if it seems too loose, fold in an extra tablespoon of flour before adding the fruit. Tossing the fruit in a spoonful of flour before adding also helps.

attrs.avoid: Avoid overbaking; a dry Dundee cake cannot be rescued.
attrs.fix: Remove from the oven as soon as the skewer comes out clean. While still warm, pierce the top several times with a skewer and spoon over 1 to 2 tablespoons of whisky or orange juice to add moisture.
